title: The day is short (Avot 2:15)
hookLine: Rabbi Tarfon: the day is short, the work is great, the workers are lazy
carry: start with the thing that matters most

lines: A FOREMAN ON A BUILDING SITE.
cards: It's four in the afternoon. You look at your list. Somehow the easy things got done: the emails, the small errands, a very thorough reorganization of your desk.
And the one hard thing, the thing that actually mattered, is still at the top of the list, untouched. The light is already changing.

Rabbi Tarfon, a priest who lived through the years when the Temple was destroyed, knew that four o'clock feeling. He put it into five short phrases that sound like a foreman shouting across a building site.

teach.b: The day is short. The work is great. The workers are lazy.
The reward is great. And the master of the house is pressing. Start with his world.
In ancient Israel, a day laborer worked from sunrise to sundown, and the Torah said he had to be paid before the sun went down. So the whole day had a clock on it. When the light's gone, it's gone.

teach.h: A LIFE IS A WORKING DAY.
teach.b: Now read the saying as a picture of a life. The day is short: a lifetime goes faster than anyone expects. The work is great: so much to learn, so much good to do, so many people who need something.
The workers are lazy: that's people, honestly. Not wicked. Just distracted, tired, reorganizing the desk.
The reward is great: the work is worth it, more than anyone can see. And the master of the house is pressing: God, in this picture, is the owner of the field, and there's a gentle urgency in the air.
Notice what Rabbi Tarfon doesn't say. Not you're a failure. Not it's hopeless.
He names the situation as plainly as a foreman would, and trusts you to do the math.
If the day is short and the work is great, you start with the thing that matters most.
And if that sounds like a lot of pressure, hold on. Tomorrow, the very next line of Pirkei Avot, from the same Rabbi Tarfon, lets you breathe again.

how: Rabbi Tarfon's saying is often quoted in Jewish teaching as a reminder that life is brief and there is much good to do, and it is usually paired with the saying that follows it.

o: a Levite singer who led the psalms in the Temple
a Roman-era judge who ruled on day laborers' wages
a priest-sage: the day is short, the work is great

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.

s: a day laborer in ancient Israel was paid before sundown
the Torah said he had to be paid that same day.
Rabbi Tarfon calls the workers wicked
he calls them lazy: distracted, tired, human.
Rabbi Tarfon lived through the time the Temple was destroyed
he was a priest, and served there as a young man.

games.q: it's four in the afternoon. the easy tasks are done and the hard one hasn't been touched. what does Rabbi Tarfon's saying suggest?
o: tidy a few more small things first.
start the hard thing now. the day is short.
leave it for tomorrow. there's always tomorrow.
games.why: the day is short and the work is great, he says. if the light is going, start with what matters most.

practice: Let today's list come to mind, and notice the item you keep circling: the hard one, the one that matters. Don't feel guilty about it; just see it clearly.
Then picture the first five minutes of doing it: where you'll sit, what you'll open, the first sentence, the first call, the first step.

wordCard.voice: Rabbi Tarfon, the priest who named the day short, the work great, the workers lazy, the reward great, and the master of the house pressing.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: the day is short, and the work is great.

carryVoice: Your line: start with the thing that matters most. The light doesn't wait. Two hundred sixty-three days in.
